title: Where the blood goes
goal: Explain how cardiac output is shared out in exercise: vasodilation in working muscle, constriction in the gut and kidneys, functional sympatholysis and the muscle pump.

steps.title: Sharing out the cardiac output
steps.text:
At rest, skeletal muscle gets about a fifth of Q. At max it gets most of it [[c:bf-table]]:

| mL·min⁻¹ | rest | max |
|---|---|---|
| skeletal muscle | 1200 | 12,500 |
| gut | 1400 | 600 |
| kidneys | 1100 | 600 |
| brain | 750 | 750 |
| skin | 500 | 1900 |
| total Q | 5800 | 17,500 |

(Textbook values; heart and other organs left out.)

Vessels in working muscle widen, while sympathetic drive narrows those to the gut and kidneys: their flow can fall to a quarter of rest, yet they keep their O₂ supply by extracting more [[c:bf-visceral]]. Brain flow holds steady; skin gets more, to shed heat.

claims.text: In exercise, blood flow is redistributed: much more to muscle and skin, less to the gut and kidneys, and about the same to the brain.

evidence.quote: Only the brain receives a more or less constant supply of blood whether you are active, resting, thinking, or engaged in any other activity.
During exercise, the body distributes more blood to the body surface where it can dissipate the excess heat generated by increased activity into the environment.
Simultaneously, vasoconstriction occurs in the vessels leading to the kidneys and most of the digestive and reproductive organs.

claims.text: In heavy exercise, sympathetic vasoconstriction can cut renal and splanchnic blood flow to about 25% of rest, with O₂ uptake kept up by higher extraction.

evidence.quote: For example, as a result of sympathetic vasoconstriction, renal and splanchnic blood flow can both fall to ∼25% of resting values during heavy exercise in humans, but oxygen consumption in these tissues is preserved by marked increases in extraction

steps.title: Muscle's share of cardiac output
steps.problem: Using the table, what share of cardiac output goes to skeletal muscle at rest and at max?
steps: Max: 12,500 ÷ 17,500 = 0.71, so 71%. In trained athletes with a bigger Q, the share is higher still.

steps.title: Opening the taps in working muscle
steps.text:
Flow through a vessel depends on pressure and resistance, and the one thing the body can change quickly is the vessel's radius [[c:bf-radius]]. Widening, [vasodilation](g:vasodilation), lowers resistance, so more blood flows at the same pressure.

Working muscle dilates enormously. In one-leg kicking, the knee extensors took about **2.5 L·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹** at max, about 100 times resting flow, and flow tracked the muscles' O₂ demand [[c:bf-max-flow]]. At low intensities that rise came from dilation alone; higher pressure only helped at high work rates.

What opens the vessels? Candidates include adenosine, ATP, nitric oxide and potassium, from working muscle and the vessel walls. No single one explains it [[c:bf-no-single]]: several signals overlap.

claims.text: Of the factors setting vascular resistance, only vessel radius can change quickly, through vasoconstriction and vasodilation.

evidence.quote: Only one of these factors, the radius, can be changed rapidly by vasoconstriction and vasodilation, thus dramatically impacting resistance and flow.

claims.text: Maximally working human muscle can take about 2.5 (2–3) L·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, about 100 times rest; flow follows O₂ demand, and the vascular bed is not the limit on O₂ transport.

evidence.quote: With a mean estimated weight of the knee extensors of 2.30 kg the perfusion of maximally exercising skeletal muscle of man is thus in the order of 2.5 l kg-1 min-1, and the oxygen uptake 0.35 l kg-1 min-1.
The hyperaemia at low work intensities is due to vasodilatation, and an elevated mean arterial blood pressure only contributes to the linear increase in flow at high work rates.
Considering the size of the knee-extensor muscles, perfusion during peak effort may amount to 2-3 L kg(-1) min(-1), i.e. approximately 100-fold elevation from rest.

claims.text: No single dominant dilator mechanism explains exercise hyperaemia.

evidence.quote: At this time, no one dominant dilator mechanism accounts for exercise hyperemia.

steps.title: Functional sympatholysis: the nerves are overruled
steps.text:
In hard exercise, sympathetic nerves fire at vessels all over the body, working muscle included. Yet inside contracting muscle their constricting effect is blunted: [functional sympatholysis](g:functional-sympatholysis) [[c:bf-sympatholysis-def]]. Local signals overrule the nerves, so the gut and kidneys clamp down while working muscle stays open.

Not completely, though. When a large muscle mass works hard, as in running or cycling, sympathetic constriction also limits flow to the working muscles, and that is what holds blood pressure up [[c:bf-restraint]]. Muscle vessels could take more blood than the heart can pump, so something has to ration it.

How sympatholysis works is not fully understood, and even the name is argued over, since some read it as a total loss of nervous control [[c:bf-sympatholysis-debate]].

claims.text: In contracting muscle, the vasoconstrictor effect of sympathetic nerves is blunted (functional sympatholysis).

evidence.quote: In small muscle group exercise an elevation in MSNA may not cause vasoconstriction (functional sympatholysis).

This lack of a rise in perfusion pressure demonstrated that the ability of the sympathetic nerves to evoke vasoconstriction in contracting skeletal muscles was either blunted or eliminated by contractions.

claims.text: In exercise with a large muscle mass, sympathetic activity limits blood flow to the working muscles too, which maintains blood pressure.

evidence.quote: However, when engaging a large fraction of the muscle mass more intensely during exercise, the MSNA has an important functional role in maintaining blood pressure by limiting blood flow also to exercising muscles.

Additionally, complex interactions between the sympathetic nervous system and the microcirculation facilitate high levels of systemic oxygen extraction and permit just enough sympathetic control of blood flow to contracting muscles to regulate blood pressure during large muscle mass exercise in humans.

claims.text: The mechanism of functional sympatholysis is not settled, and the term itself is debated.

evidence.quote: The mechanism for functional sympatholysis is still unknown.

The term functional sympatholysis has been the matter of some debate because some investigators believe that implicit in this term is the absolute elimination of all sympathetic control of blood flow to contracting skeletal muscle.

steps.title: The muscle pump
steps.text:
Leg veins have one-way valves (anatomy module). Each contraction squeezes the veins inside the muscle and pushes blood towards the heart: the [muscle pump](g:muscle-pump).

It gives the very first rise in muscle blood flow when exercise starts; flow gets halfway to its new level within 2–10 s [[c:bf-pump-onset]]. Rapid vasodilation, detectable within 2 s, adds to this early rise [[c:bf-rapid-dilation]].

It keeps working after the start. By emptying the veins it keeps venous pressure low, which widens the pressure difference driving blood through a working leg, and it helps refill the heart [[c:bf-pump-gradient]]. That refilling is the venous return that Frank–Starling turns into a bigger stroke volume.

claims.text: Muscle blood flow rises within seconds of starting exercise (half-time 2–10 s), the muscle pump giving the very first increase.

evidence.quote: The onset of hyperaemia is very fast at the start of exercise with T 1/2 of 2-10 s related to the power output with the muscle pump bringing about the very first increase in blood flow.

claims.text: Besides the muscle pump, a rapid vasodilation detectable within 2 s contributes to the early rise in flow.

evidence.quote: We conclude that a functional muscle pump does exist in the human forearm in vivo, but that a rapid vasodilation detectable within 2 s also contributes to the early exercise hyperemia.

claims.text: The muscle pump keeps venous pressure low, raising the perfusion pressure gradient across a working limb, and aids venous return and cardiac filling.

evidence.quote: These studies indicate that the muscle pump operates to increase the perfusion pressure gradient across a dependent exercising limb by keeping venous pressure low. It also facilitates venous return and cardiac filling

points: At rest muscle gets about a fifth of Q; at max most of it. Gut and kidney flow fall to about a quarter of rest; brain flow holds steady; skin gets more for heat.
Flow is set by pressure and resistance, and the body changes resistance through vessel radius: working muscle can take about 2.5 L·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, about 100 times rest.
Several local dilator signals act together; no single one explains it.
Functional sympatholysis blunts sympathetic constriction in working muscle, but in whole-body exercise some constriction remains and rations flow to hold blood pressure.
The muscle pump starts the rise in flow within seconds, keeps venous pressure low and refills the heart.

variants.stem: At maximal effort, a cyclist's cardiac output is 30 L·min⁻¹, and 25 L·min⁻¹ of it goes to skeletal muscle. What share of Q is that?

options.why: That is the share going everywhere else (5 ÷ 30).
This divides Q by muscle flow (30 ÷ 25). Share = part ÷ whole.
A decimal slip: 25 ÷ 30 = 0.83, which is 83%, not 8.3%.

variants.stem: At maximal effort, a runner's cardiac output is 22 L·min⁻¹, and 18 L·min⁻¹ of it goes to skeletal muscle. What share of Q is that?

options.why: That is the share going everywhere else (4 ÷ 22).
This divides Q by muscle flow (22 ÷ 18). Share = part ÷ whole.
A decimal slip: 18 ÷ 22 = 0.82, which is 82%, not 8.2%.

variants.stem: From rest to maximal exercise, what happens to blood flow to the brain?

options.text: It stays about the same
options.why: Right: the brain gets a more or less constant supply, about 750 mL·min⁻¹ in the textbook table.

options.text: It halves, to feed the muscles
options.why: Brain flow is protected; the cuts come from the gut and kidneys.

options.text: It roughly doubles
options.why: It stays about the same while total Q triples or more.

options.text: It rises about tenfold
options.why: That is what happens in working muscle, not in the brain.

variants.stem: On a hard bike leg, a triathlete's cardiac output is three times her resting value. Which of these keeps about the same blood flow as at rest?

options.text: The brain
options.why: Right: the brain gets a more or less constant supply whether you rest or exercise.

options.text: The kidneys
options.why: Kidney flow falls, to about a quarter of rest in heavy exercise, through sympathetic constriction.

options.text: The skin
options.why: Skin flow rises in exercise, to shed heat.

options.text: The leg muscles
options.why: Working muscle flow rises many times over.

variants.stem: Working muscle can take about 2.5 L·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Suppose a cyclist works 15 kg of leg muscle all out and every kilogram took that much, while his maximal cardiac output is 25 L·min⁻¹. What follows?

options.text: His muscles could take more blood than his heart can pump
options.why: Right: 15 × 2.5 = 37.5 L·min⁻¹, well above 25. In whole-body exercise the heart, not the muscle's vessels, is the limit, and flow must be rationed.

options.text: His muscles would get all the flow they can take
options.why: 37.5 L·min⁻¹ is more than the 25 L·min⁻¹ his heart can deliver.

options.text: His cardiac output would rise to 37.5 L·min⁻¹ to match
options.why: Q can't rise above its maximum; demand doesn't create pumping capacity.

options.text: His muscle vessels are the main limit on his VO₂max
options.why: The reverse: the muscle's vascular bed can take more than the heart supplies, so it isn't the limit.

variants.solution: Possible muscle flow = 15 kg × 2.5 L·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ = 37.5 L·min⁻¹ > maximal Q of 25 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: Working muscle can take about 2.5 L·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Suppose a runner works 12 kg of leg muscle all out and every kilogram took that much, while her maximal cardiac output is 22 L·min⁻¹. What follows?

options.text: Her muscles could take more blood than her heart can pump
options.why: Right: 12 × 2.5 = 30 L·min⁻¹, well above 22. In whole-body exercise the heart, not the muscle's vessels, is the limit, and flow must be rationed.

options.text: Her muscles would get all the flow they can take
options.why: 30 L·min⁻¹ is more than the 22 L·min⁻¹ her heart can deliver.

options.text: Her cardiac output would rise to 30 L·min⁻¹ to match
options.why: Q can't rise above its maximum; demand doesn't create pumping capacity.

options.text: Her muscle vessels are the main limit on her VO₂max
options.why: The reverse: the muscle's vascular bed can take more than the heart supplies, so it isn't the limit.

variants.solution: Possible muscle flow = 12 kg × 2.5 L·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ = 30 L·min⁻¹ > maximal Q of 22 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: What best describes what opens the small arteries in a runner's working leg muscles?

options.text: Several local signals acting together, none dominant
options.why: Right: adenosine, ATP, nitric oxide, potassium and others all play a part; no single dilator accounts for it.

options.text: Lactate, acting alone
options.why: Lactate barely rises in easy exercise, yet muscle flow rises a lot, so it can't be the one essential signal.

options.text: Sympathetic nerves dilating them
options.why: Sympathetic nerves constrict vessels; the dilation in working muscle is local.

options.text: Higher blood pressure stretching them open
options.why: At low intensities flow rises by dilation alone; higher pressure only adds at high work rates.

variants.stem: In a hard 4 km pursuit, sympathetic activity is high throughout the body. Why do the gut's vessels narrow while the working quadriceps' vessels stay open?

options.text: Local signals in working muscle blunt the sympathetic constriction
options.why: Right: that is functional sympatholysis; in resting beds like the gut the constriction works fully.

options.text: Muscle vessels have no sympathetic nerves
options.why: They do, and the nerves fire; their effect is blunted inside contracting muscle.

options.text: The vagus nerve dilates muscle vessels
options.why: The vagus acts on the heart; it doesn't dilate muscle vessels.

options.text: Higher pressure in the legs forces them open
options.why: Pressure helps at high work rates, but it can't explain why one bed constricts and the other doesn't.

variants.stem: A runner's leg muscles could take more blood than her heart can pump. What best explains why her blood pressure doesn't collapse in a hard race?

options.text: Sympathetic constriction also rations flow to the working muscles
options.why: Right: in large-muscle-mass exercise, sympathetic activity limits flow to working muscle too, and that maintains blood pressure.

options.text: Her brain flow falls to free up blood
options.why: Brain flow stays about constant in exercise.

options.text: Her heart rate climbs beyond its maximum
options.why: HR can't exceed HRmax; Q has a ceiling.

options.text: Her muscle vessels can't widen much beyond rest
options.why: They can widen hugely, up to about 100 times resting flow; that's why rationing is needed.

variants.stem: Two triathletes cross the line after a hard run. One stops and stands still; the other keeps walking. Whose venous return to the heart is better supported, and why?

options.text: The walker's: contracting legs keep pumping blood back
options.why: Right: walking keeps the muscle pump going, emptying the leg veins towards the heart.

options.text: The one standing: resting lets blood return
options.why: Standing still lets blood pool in the leg veins; nothing is pushing it back up.

options.text: No difference: the heart sucks blood back up
options.why: The heart doesn't pull blood up the legs; venous return relies on pressure and the pumps.

options.text: The one standing: their heart rate falls faster
options.why: A falling HR doesn't move blood up out of the legs.

variants.stem: In the first seconds of pedalling, what causes the very first rise in leg muscle blood flow?

options.text: The muscle pump, helped by rapid vasodilation
options.why: Right: the pump gives the very first increase, and a rapid dilation within 2 s adds to it.

options.text: Sympathetic nerves dilating the arteries
options.why: Sympathetic nerves constrict vessels; they don't drive the early rise in muscle flow.

options.text: A sharp rise in arterial pressure
options.why: Arterial pressure changes little at the start of light work; pressure only adds at high work rates.

options.text: Lactate building up in the muscle
options.why: Too slow: flow rises within 2–10 s, before lactate has built up, and lactate isn't the essential dilator.
